stories.head: Trump says Iran war 'effectively over' after meeting Qatar's prime minister
stories.say: After meeting Qatar's prime minister on Monday, Donald Trump said further strikes on Iran were quite unlikely, though US forces remained locked and loaded.
stories.stand: Donald Trump said more US strikes on Iran were unlikely, while Tehran insisted the US must first end its naval blockade and lift sanctions.
body: Donald Trump said on Monday that "Iran, militarily, is effectively over" and that further US strikes were quite unlikely. He spoke after meeting Qatar's prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, at the White House.

Trump wrote that the US was seeing positive momentum towards ending the conflict, but said US forces remained locked and loaded. Qatar has acted as a mediator between Washington and Tehran. AFP reported it was Trump's first meeting with a foreign leader since his party's midterm losses.

On Sunday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was no progress to report and called some of Iran's demands unrealistic. On Monday, Iran's foreign ministry spokesman, Esmail Baghaei, said its offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days, if the US meets Tehran's demands, still stood.

Iran says the US must end its naval blockade and lift sanctions before talks resume. Iranian state media said the US struck Qeshm Island overnight into Monday. The US military has not publicly acknowledged strikes inside Iran, AFP reported.

stories.head: Trump expects to meet Putin and Xi together at APEC summit in China
stories.say: Donald Trump says he expects to sit down with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping at the APEC summit in Shenzhen later this month, with Iran on the agenda.
stories.stand: Donald Trump says one of his meetings at the summit in Shenzhen will be with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, though talks are not yet confirmed.
body: Donald Trump said on Sunday that he expects to meet Russia's Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping together during his trip to China. The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit is due to be held in Shenzhen on 18 and 19 November.
Trump told reporters the leaders would discuss denuclearisation and that the US was trying to end the war in Iran. The three-way meeting has not been confirmed.

The Kremlin said last week that work was under way to arrange the talks. Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said there was a general understanding among the participants that such a meeting would be worthwhile, Breitbart reported.

Euronews reported that a fragile trade truce between the US and China is due to expire in January. Analysts quoted by Euronews doubted the leaders would agree anything substantive, as their interests are at odds.

stories.head: Drone attack on Iraqi Kurdish gas field causes widespread blackouts
stories.say: A drone strike on the Khor Mor gas field on Sunday night knocked up to 2.8 gigawatts off the power grid in Iraq's Kurdistan region, officials said.
stories.stand: A drone strike on the Khor Mor gas field halted production and cut up to 2.8 gigawatts from the Kurdistan region's power grid.
body: A drone attack on the Khor Mor gas field in Iraq's Kurdistan region on Sunday night started a fire and caused widespread blackouts, officials said. The field is in Sulaimaniyah province.

Omid Ahmed, spokesman for the regional electricity ministry, said 2.5 to 2.8 gigawatts had been lost from the grid. Hospitals and water stations were being supplied from hydropower and fuel-powered plants.

Dana Gas, a joint operator of the field, said on Monday that production remained suspended. It said the fire had been put out and no staff were hurt. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered a joint investigation with Kurdish authorities.
No group has claimed responsibility. Kurdish authorities have blamed Iran-backed militias for earlier attacks on the field, including one in November 2025, The National reported.

stories.head: Five killed in Gaza as storm brings sand embankment down on tents
stories.say: Five people, including children, were killed on Sunday when a sand embankment collapsed onto tents for displaced families in central Gaza after heavy rain, rescuers said.
stories.stand: Rescuers say the collapse in Deir el-Balah followed heavy rain that flooded about 70,000 tents sheltering displaced people.
body: Five people, including children, were killed on Sunday when a sand embankment collapsed onto tents for displaced people in Deir el-Balah, central Gaza, rescuers said. The collapse followed heavy rain from the first winter storm of the season.
Mahmud Bassal, spokesman for Gaza's civil defence, said teams were searching for missing people. Al Jazeera reported that residents dug with their hands because rescuers lacked specialist equipment.
Gaza's government media office said about 70,000 tents had been flooded. It held Israel, the United States and the international community responsible.
Save the Children said Israel had repeatedly blocked the entry of caravans, which the ceasefire had envisaged as an alternative to tents. The ceasefire took effect in October 2025.

stories.head: Mexico arrests alleged Jalisco cartel cell leader 'R2' after shootout
stories.say: Mexican forces have captured Rafael Álvarez Ayala, known as R2, an alleged Jalisco cartel cell leader wanted in the US, after a shootout near Guadalajara on Sunday.
stories.stand: Rafael Álvarez Ayala, wanted in Mexico and the US, was wounded and detained in Zapopan along with 19 others, officials said.
body: Mexican forces arrested Rafael Álvarez Ayala, known as "R2", an alleged leader of a Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) cell, on Sunday. The arrest took place in Zapopan, in the Guadalajara area.

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said he was wounded in a shootout and was receiving medical care. In all, 19 other people were detained. The US Drug Enforcement Administration said intelligence it shared helped locate him.
He faces a Mexican arrest warrant for aggravated homicide and a separate warrant for extradition to the US. Latin Times reported he faces US drug trafficking and firearms charges.
Authorities link his cell, Los Rs, to the 2025 killing of Carlos Manzo, the mayor of Uruapan. His brother Ramón, alias "R1", was arrested in July 2026.

stories.head: Pope Leo tells Argentina's leaders the economy must serve people
stories.say: On the first papal visit to Argentina since 1987, Pope Leo told leaders the economy must serve the person, and urged help for retirees and the unemployed.
stories.stand: Leo XIV is making the first papal visit to Argentina since 1987, in Pope Francis's homeland, and met President Javier Milei at the Casa Rosada.
body: Pope Leo XIV arrived in Buenos Aires on Sunday for the first papal visit to Argentina since 1987. President Javier Milei welcomed him, and the two met at the Casa Rosada presidential palace.
In a speech to leaders, the pope said the economy must serve the person, not the other way round. He backed private initiative but urged help for the unemployed, retirees and struggling workers.

He also called for investment in education and universities, and said Argentina's democracy must be safeguarded. Milei called Leo an exceptional figure and said he hoped the visit would bring a message of peace.

Milei has cut public spending sharply to curb inflation. About 300,000 formal jobs have been lost since his reforms began, AP reported. Argentina is the second stop on a 12-day tour that began in Uruguay; the pope leaves for Peru on Wednesday.

stories.head: Earthquake in central Japan injures more than 20 people
stories.say: A magnitude 5.7 earthquake shook central Japan early on Sunday, injuring more than 20 people, and officials warned that further strong tremors could follow.
stories.stand: The quake struck Shizuoka Prefecture early on Sunday, shattering shop windows, and officials warned of possible strong tremors in the following week.
body: A magnitude 5.7 earthquake struck central Japan at 1:04am local time on Sunday, injuring more than 20 people, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency and local media. The epicentre was in Shizuoka Prefecture, about 40km deep.
Injuries were reported in Aichi and Shizuoka prefectures. Some people were hurt falling on stairs as they fled. Shop windows shattered and glass was scattered across streets.

No tsunami warning was issued. The agency warned of possible strong quakes over the following week, especially in the next two to three days. Official Ayataka Ebita said no apparent change had been detected in the Nankai Trough.
Shinkansen bullet trains slowed as a precaution, and some local services were suspended. The quake was not felt in Tokyo.

stories.head: Firefighting helicopter crashes into Borneo river, killing one crew member
stories.say: A water-bombing helicopter fighting forest fires on Borneo plunged into a river on Sunday, killing an Indonesian crew member; an Australian and a New Zealander survived.
stories.stand: An Australian and a New Zealander survived when the water-bombing helicopter came down in South Kalimantan, the second such crash in Kalimantan in a week.
body: A water-bombing helicopter crashed into the Barito River in South Kalimantan, Indonesia, on Sunday, killing an Indonesian crew member. It was scooping water to fight forest fires on Borneo.
An Australian and a New Zealander on board survived. They were pulled from the water and treated at a military hospital, ABC News reported. Rescue teams later found the body of the third crew member.
The Jakarta Post said the aircraft was a Eurocopter EC225LP Super Puma. Indonesia's disaster agency, BNPB, said it would support an official investigation and review aerial firefighting operations.

It was the second such crash in Kalimantan in a week. On 4 November, an Indonesian Army helicopter crashed while loading water in Central Kalimantan, killing three crew. Officials describe this as Indonesia's worst forest fire season in more than a decade.

stories.head: Seven killed and more than 100 hurt as trains collide near Cairo
stories.say: At least seven people were killed and more than 100 injured on Sunday when one passenger train ran into the back of another on the edge of Cairo.
stories.stand: A train bound for Fayoum hit the back of a Cairo-to-Aswan service in Giza province, and President Sisi has ordered an urgent investigation.
body: At least seven people were killed when two passenger trains collided in al-Ayyat district, Giza province, on the edge of Cairo, on Sunday. More than 100 people were injured, the health ministry said.

Officials said a train running between Giza and Fayoum struck the rear of another train heading from Cairo to Aswan, which derailed. Al Jazeera reported that more than 70 ambulances helped take casualties to hospital.
President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi ordered an urgent investigation and said anyone found negligent should be held accountable. The public prosecutor is examining the technical causes.
Al-Ayyat was the site of Egypt's worst rail disaster, when a train fire killed more than 370 people in 2002.

stories.head: Death toll from migrant boat sinking off Senegal rises to 39
stories.say: At least 39 people died when a migrant boat bound for Spain sank off northwestern Senegal on Saturday, with only one passenger rescued alive.
stories.stand: Only one person survived when the pirogue heading for Spain overturned off the Lompoul dunes, and a rights group wants a parliamentary inquiry.
body: At least 39 people died when a small boat carrying migrants sank off northwestern Senegal, Al Jazeera and News.az reported. Only one passenger was rescued alive, and others are still missing.

The wooden pirogue had left Saint-Louis bound for Spain. It overturned on Saturday off the Lompoul dunes in Kebemer department, about 180km north of Dakar. The toll rose from an initial 21 to 34, then 39.
The rights group Action for Human Rights and Friendship (ADHA) called for a parliamentary inquiry. President Bassirou Diomaye Faye offered condolences and pledged action against traffickers.

The Interior Ministry did not say how many people were on board. On Spain's El Hierro island, authorities declared an emergency on Saturday after more than 3,300 people arrived on about 30 boats since the start of November.

stories.head: Krakow gunman dies in hospital as Poland treats attack as terrorism
stories.say: The gunman who killed six people in Krakow's Main Square on Saturday has died in hospital, police said, as prosecutors treat the attack as a terrorist offence.
stories.stand: Prosecutors say Saturday's shooting in Krakow's Main Square, which killed six people, constitutes a terrorist offence; the suspect died on Monday.
body: The suspect in Saturday's mass shooting in Krakow's Main Square died in hospital on Monday, police said. He had been in critical condition after several operations, having been wounded by police.
Six people were killed and 15 injured when a gunman opened fire in the historic centre of Poland's second-largest city. ABC News reported that a British man and an Austrian woman were among the dead.

Polish prosecutors are treating the attack as a terrorist offence. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the 24-year-old suspect held very radical, ultranationalist views. Police said the bodies of his father, mother and sister were found at the family home.
The square reopened on Sunday evening, and Poland held two days of national mourning.

stories.head: Moldova opens power line to Romania to cut reliance on Russian supply
stories.say: Moldova switched on a new high-voltage power line to Romania on Sunday, linking it to the European grid and reducing its reliance on supply from Transnistria.
stories.stand: The 158km line links Moldova directly to the European grid and reduces its dependence on a power plant in pro-Moscow Transnistria.
body: Moldova switched on a new 400kV power line on Sunday linking it to Romania and the European grid. Officials called it the "energy independence line".
The 158km Vulcanesti-Chisinau line lets Moldova reduce its reliance on the Cuciurgan power plant in Transnistria, a pro-Moscow separatist region. It was financed by a €61 million World Bank loan.
President Maia Sandu said Moscow had used energy to blackmail Moldova for decades, and that two more power lines to Romania were on the way. EU commissioner Marta Kos attended the launch.
Al Jazeera said the line opened two years later than originally promised. In October, Moldova's parliament approved a state of emergency until 20 November to ease gas shortages.

stories.head: Russell Brand jailed for 10 years and six months
stories.say: Russell Brand was jailed on Monday for ten and a half years, after a jury found him guilty of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others.
stories.stand: The comedian was sentenced at Southwark Crown Court for one rape and three sexual assaults committed between 2004 and 2009.
body: Russell Brand was jailed for 10 years and six months at Southwark Crown Court on Monday. A jury convicted him last week of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

STV News reported that the term is made up of nine years for the rape and 18 months for the sexual assaults. Yahoo News UK said he must serve two-thirds of the term before he can be considered for release. The Metropolitan Police said he will be on the sex offenders' register for life.

The rape victim was a 21-year-old fan he met at a stand-up show in 2009. The other three women were a radio worker, a Channel 4 worker and an MTV worker, ITV News reported. He was cleared of two counts of rape and one of attempted indecent assault.

Mr Justice Bennathan told Brand he had become a sexual predator. Brand denied all the charges and said the encounters were consensual. Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy of the Met said no one is above the law.

stories.head: Jon Venables to stay in prison after Parole Board review
stories.say: One of James Bulger's killers, Jon Venables, will remain behind bars after telling a Parole Board panel he needed more offending work in custody and was not seeking release.
stories.stand: The Parole Board said it was not satisfied he was suitable for release; Venables himself said he was not seeking to be freed.
body: Jon Venables, one of the two boys who murdered James Bulger in 1993, will stay in prison. A summary of the Parole Board's decision was published on Monday.
The board held the review in private. Venables told the panel at the start that he accepted he needed further offending work in custody and was not seeking release, ITV News and RTÉ reported.

The panel heard from probation officers, three psychologists and a psychiatrist. All but one said he should remain in prison. ITV News said the panel was concerned about how open he would be under supervision.

Venables and Robert Thompson were both 10 when they abducted two-year-old James from a shopping centre in Bootle, Merseyside. Venables was released in 2001 and recalled in 2010 and again in 2017 over indecent images of children.

stories.head: Suspended councillor guilty over post about melting down Nigerians
stories.say: A suspended Reform UK councillor in Sunderland has been given a community order after a judge ruled his Facebook post about Nigerians was grossly offensive.
stories.stand: Glenn Gibbins, 66, was convicted under the Communications Act 2003 and given 150 hours of unpaid work. He plans to appeal.
body: Glenn Gibbins, a suspended Reform UK councillor on Sunderland City Council, was found guilty on Monday over a Facebook post about Nigerians. The trial took place at South Tyneside Magistrates' Court.

The post, made in March 2024 before he was elected, said Nigerians should be melted down to fill in pot holes, ITV News reported. He was convicted of sending a grossly offensive message under the Communications Act 2003.

District Judge Zoe Passfield gave him a 12-month community order with 150 hours of unpaid work. She said the post was not a genuine expression of political views and so was not protected as free expression.
Gibbins, 66, called the post a joke. His legal team said he will appeal to the crown court. Reform UK suspended him after the post came to light.

stories.head: Royal Navy commissions its first squadron of uncrewed boats
stories.say: The Royal Navy has commissioned its first frontline squadron of uncrewed boats in Portsmouth, with about 180 sailors operating remotely piloted Kraken and Rattler craft.
stories.stand: The 1st Autonomous Squadron was commissioned in Portsmouth, part of what the navy calls a move towards a hybrid fleet.
body: The Royal Navy has commissioned its first squadron dedicated to uncrewed boats on frontline operations. The 1st Autonomous Squadron was commissioned at a ceremony in Portsmouth on 5 November, Navy Lookout reported.
The squadron has about 180 personnel. It operates Rattler boats, used mainly for training, and Kraken K3 Scout boats, which have a range of about 600 miles that can be extended to about 1,100 miles.

ITV News said Rattler boats have been trialled escorting warships in Scotland while piloted from 500 miles away. It reported £1.5 billion of funding over four years for what the navy calls a hybrid navy.
Fleet Commander Vice-Admiral Steve Moorhouse read the commissioning orders. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the threat environment is fundamentally different from that of recent decades.

stories.head: Army carries out controlled explosion on package sent to Asda HQ
stories.say: Staff were evacuated from Asda's Leeds headquarters on Monday after a suspicious package was sent there, and an Army bomb disposal team carried out a controlled explosion.
stories.stand: Police said no one was harmed and there was no wider threat to the public, but roads in central Leeds stayed shut into the evening.
body: Asda's head office in Leeds was evacuated on Monday after a suspicious package was sent to the building. An Army bomb disposal team carried out a controlled explosion on it.

West Yorkshire Police said reports of the package came in at 11.16am at Asda House on Great Wilson Street, Brit Brief reported. Police said no one was harmed and there was no wider threat to the public.
Roads including Victoria Road, Meadow Lane, Neville Street, Bridge End and Great Wilson Street were closed. Police said closures would stay in place through the evening rush hour.
No arrests were reported. Police said further investigation was continuing.

stories.head: Arrests over Bonfire Night disorder in North Shields rise to 17
stories.say: Northumbria Police have now arrested seventeen people, aged from twelve to sixty-six, over Bonfire Night disorder in the Meadow Well area of North Shields.
stories.stand: Police say the trouble was fuelled by a false rumour that a building would become a house in multiple occupation.
body: Northumbria Police have arrested 17 people over disorder in the Meadow Well area of North Shields on Bonfire Night. Those arrested are aged between 12 and 66.

On Thursday 5 November a building on Waterville Road was attacked with fireworks and rammed with a car, police said. Five police cars and three fire engines were damaged, and emergency crews were attacked.
Police said the trouble was linked to misinformation that the building would become a house in multiple occupation. They said it is planned as a supermarket, ITV News and Brit Brief reported.
Fifteen people are on police bail and two face no further action. Chief Superintendent Daniel Whyte said more arrests were expected.

stories.head: Venues given planning tools to prepare for Martyn's Law
stories.say: The Security Industry Authority has published planning tools to help venues and events get ready for Martyn's Law, the anti-terror rules expected to take effect in spring 2027.
stories.stand: The regulator released a standard tier planning tool and an enhanced tier template, and is asking for feedback before 23 December.
body: The Security Industry Authority (SIA) has published new tools to help venues and events prepare for Martyn's Law. The law is expected to come into force in spring 2027, the SIA said on Monday.

A planning tool for standard tier premises covers evacuation, lockdown, communication and invacuation, which means moving people to safe areas inside a building. A template for enhanced tier premises and events covers documenting security measures.

When the law takes effect, premises and events in scope must notify the SIA. Events are in scope only if 800 or more people are expected at the busiest time, entry is controlled and the public can attend.
The SIA wants feedback on the tools before 23 December. Laura Gibb, its executive director for Martyn's Law, said the materials were a first step.

stories.head: Dense fog warning renewed for central and eastern England
stories.say: The Met Office renewed its yellow fog warning for Monday night into Tuesday, saying visibility could fall below a hundred metres and disrupt travel across much of England and north Wales.
stories.stand: A yellow warning runs until 10am on Tuesday, after fog on Sunday night and Monday morning hit travel in the South East and east.
body: The Met Office has issued a yellow fog warning from 6pm on Monday until 10am on Tuesday. It covers large parts of the Midlands, eastern and northern England, Greater Manchester and north Wales.
The forecaster said fog would become dense overnight, with visibility below 100 metres. It warned of delays to transport and difficult travel conditions.

An earlier warning ran from Sunday evening until 11am on Monday, from York to Bath and across much of the South East. ITV News said visibility could fall to 50 metres or less, with delays to buses, trains and flights.
On Saturday evening a crash involving more than 30 vehicles closed the M20 in Kent for nearly 12 hours, ITV News reported. Two people were seriously injured.

stories.head: West Highland Line shut for nine days for £13m upgrade
stories.say: Trains on the West Highland Line are being replaced by buses until Tuesday the seventeenth of November while Network Rail carries out a thirteen million pound upgrade.
stories.stand: Network Rail is replacing worn track and repairing bridges between Helensburgh, Fort William and Mallaig.
body: The West Highland Line in Scotland is closed for nine days for a £13 million upgrade. The work began on Monday 9 November and runs until Tuesday 17 November, STV News reported.
Network Rail is replacing worn track near Arisaig and Corrour and in two tunnels. It is also refurbishing Fassfern Bridge near Spean Bridge and removing a disused bridge near Loch Eil.
Buses are replacing trains between Crianlarich and Fort William and Mallaig. ScotRail urged passengers to check their journeys before travelling.
Gerry McQuade of Network Rail Scotland said the work would make the railway more reliable for passengers.

stories.say: The government has moved to give veterans' and service personnel's rail discounts legal protection, through an amendment to the Railways Bill laid on Monday.
stories.stand: Railcards give veterans and serving personnel about a third off most fares, but the discount had no statutory protection until now.
body: The government has laid an amendment to the Railways Bill to put rail discounts for veterans and service personnel on a statutory footing. Lord Hendy set it out in a written statement on Monday.
Railcards give veterans and service personnel about a third off most fares. The statement said the discount had no statutory protection until now.
Discounts for young, older and disabled passengers already have statutory protection, the Department for Transport said. The bill will also create Great British Railways.

stories.head: Burnham pledges accommodation offer for veterans sleeping rough
stories.say: Andy Burnham has promised that every veteran sleeping rough will be offered somewhere to stay before Christmas, and will write to councils in England on Armistice Day.
stories.stand: The prime minister will ask councils to plan with charities and use part of existing homelessness funding for veterans.
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged that every veteran sleeping rough will be offered accommodation before Christmas. He will write to councils in England on Armistice Day, 11 November, asking them to draw up plans with charities.
Councils will be asked to use part of £874 million in homelessness funding, LBC and ITV News reported. That sits within £4.4 billion committed over three years.
ITV News said £8.7 million would go to eight organisations for veterans' housing and specialist support. LBC said the letter would highlight councils' duties under the Armed Forces Covenant.
LBC said 4,793 people were sleeping rough in England on a single night in autumn 2025, the highest figure recorded. Burnham said no one who has served the country should be left to sleep rough.

stories.head: Inquest finds Boxing Day house fire that killed family was accidental
stories.say: A coroner has ruled that a Boxing Day fire near Stroud, which killed a mother and her two young children, was accidental and probably started by electrical devices.
stories.stand: The fire in a Gloucestershire cottage probably began with mains-powered devices in the living room, the inquest heard.
body: A coroner has ruled that the deaths of a mother and her two children in a house fire near Stroud were accidental. The inquest was held at Gloucestershire Coroner's Court on Monday, ITV News reported.
The fire broke out at about 3am on 26 December 2025 in a mid-terrace cottage on Brimscombe Hill. The children were aged seven and four.
The inquest heard the fire probably started in the living room and was likely caused by electrical devices plugged into the mains. A Christmas tree and soft furnishings probably helped it spread.

Senior coroner Katy Skerrett recorded the deaths as accidental. Police and the fire service found no suspicious circumstances. The children's father, a police officer, was driven back by the flames as he tried to reach them.

stories.stand: The Reform UK leader confirmed he had been interviewed by the standards commissioner over a £5m gift from a crypto billionaire that he did not declare.
body: Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has suggested he expects Parliament's standards commissioner to find against him over a £5m gift. He made the comments on the BBC's Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg on 8 November.

Commissioner Daniel Greenberg is investigating whether Farage should have declared the gift from crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne. Farage confirmed he had been interviewed, and ITV News said the interview lasted about 30 minutes in September.

Farage said answering questions about the inquiry could bring a letter of rebuke. Asked if he expected an adverse finding, he asked whether the establishment would find against the leader of an insurgent party.

He said the murder of Ann Widdecombe justified paying for his own security. Separately, ministers want to cap donations from Britons living overseas at £100,000, backdated to 25 March, ITV News reported.

stories.head: Burnham declines to give police watchdog full backing over Nowak case
stories.say: Andy Burnham has stopped short of backing the police watchdog over Henry Nowak's murder, saying the teenager's family had been let down.
stories.stand: The prime minister said Henry Nowak's family had been let down, after they accused police and the IOPC of misleading them.
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has declined to give the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) his full confidence over its handling of Henry Nowak's murder. Speaking on Monday, he said the 18-year-old student's family had been let down.

Burnham gave Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood his full support in reviewing the IOPC's role, ITV News reported. UnHerd reported last week that Mahmood had full confidence in the watchdog, while Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said that if the family's account was true, it looked like a cover-up.

The family say Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary and the IOPC misled them. Police initially suggested Henry was the aggressor, and bodycam footage showed officers handcuffing him after he was stabbed.

Former Lord Chancellor Alex Chalk will lead an independent review ordered by Mahmood. The IOPC says it is investigating whether officers should face disciplinary proceedings; its investigation is due to finish early next year.

stories.head: Scotland's first drug-checking service opens in Glasgow
stories.say: A service letting people dependent on illegal drugs have samples tested has opened in Glasgow, the first of its kind in Scotland, with more sites planned.
stories.stand: People dependent on illegal drugs can now have samples tested at a Glasgow site, the first of a Scottish Government pilot backed by more than £1.7m.
body: Scotland's first drug-checking service opened in Glasgow on Monday. It is on Hunter Street, on the same site as the Thistle, the UK's first official safer drug consumption facility.

People aged 18 or over who are dependent on illegal drugs can submit samples and get advice on what they contain, their strength and any contaminants. Under Home Office licence terms, it is not for general recreational testing, the Scottish Government said.

Samples go to a national laboratory at the University of Dundee, and results feed into early warning systems. Services in Aberdeen and Dundee are due to follow, and Edinburgh is working towards a site.

The pilot is backed by more than £1.7m from the Scottish Government and will be independently evaluated. Drugs Minister Maree Todd said the drug supply was increasingly unpredictable, citing potent synthetic opioids called nitazenes.

stories.head: Trump says deportations may have been too tough and floats Democrat deal
stories.say: Donald Trump has said his deportation policy might have been too tough, and that he would like to work a deal with Democrats on some undocumented immigrants.
stories.stand: In his first sit-down interview since the midterm defeat, the president also said he did not disagree with JD Vance that the Iran war cost Republicans votes.
body: President Donald Trump said his deportation policy might have been too tough, in a 60 Minutes interview with Ross Douthat broadcast on Sunday. It was his first sit-down interview since Republicans lost control of Congress.

Trump said he would like to work with Democrats on a deal for some people living in the US illegally, including some who had been there for 10 or 15 years. A White House official later told Fox News that he 'never said the word amnesty'.

Trump said he did not disagree with Vice President JD Vance's view that the Iran war and rising costs caused the losses. He said attacking Iran would historically be judged a very good decision, and he saw no reason to escalate now.
Some conservative commentators criticised the immigration remarks, Fox News reported, while Republican congresswoman Maria Elvira Salazar welcomed them.

stories.stand: Trump's immigration adviser took over on Monday after Wiles resigned following the midterm defeats; a senior Justice Department lawyer then quit.
body: President Donald Trump named Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff on Friday, replacing Susie Wiles. Miller, seen as the architect of Trump's immigration enforcement programme, was due to start on Monday.

Wiles handed in her resignation on Thursday night, and three sources told CBS News it was linked to the midterm defeats. Trump said he wanted to make a change and that Wiles had done a great job. She is moving to his political operation.
Fox News said Wiles served 21 months, the longest of any Trump chief of staff. Democratic leaders Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries condemned the appointment.
On Monday, Brett Shumate, head of the Justice Department's Civil Division, resigned with immediate effect. A source told CBS News that Miller had criticised him as not aggressive enough.

stories.head: Republican Thomas Massie files impeachment articles against Hegseth
stories.say: Republican Thomas Massie has brought eight impeachment articles against Pete Hegseth over the Iran war, which could force a House vote as soon as Wednesday.
stories.stand: The Kentucky congressman's eight articles accuse the defence secretary of waging war on Iran without authorisation; a House vote could come within days.
body: Republican congressman Thomas Massie has introduced eight articles of impeachment against Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth. He used a procedure that requires the House to consider them within two days, so a vote could come as early as Wednesday.

Three articles accuse Hegseth of waging war on Iran without congressional authorisation, CBS News reported. Others cite civilian casualties, including a strike on an Iranian school, boat strikes in the Caribbean and the capture of Venezuela's Nicolás Maduro.
Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said he was a 'hard yes'. Republican votes are needed because of the party's narrow majority, and Republican Rep French Hill said he was undecided.
Hegseth has called the articles a sham. Donald Trump said on Monday he would stand by him, Euronews reported. Removal from office would need a two-thirds Senate vote.

stories.stand: House Republicans hold leadership elections this week, with Steve Scalise facing Jim Jordan, while government funding runs out on 11 December.
body: Congress returned on Monday for the first time since the midterm elections, in which Democrats won control of both chambers. Republicans keep their majorities until the new Congress is sworn in on 3 January.

House Republicans hold leadership elections on Tuesday, CBS News reported. Speaker Mike Johnson is stepping aside, and Majority Leader Steve Scalise faces Jim Jordan for minority leader, according to CBS News and Fox News.

In the Senate, John Thune faces no announced challenger. Senator Ron Johnson is pushing to delay the Senate Republican vote, arguing the conference's size is unknown until the Mississippi and Alaska races are settled.
Government funding runs out on 11 December. House Democrats choose their leaders next week, and Hakeem Jeffries is expected to become speaker.

stories.head: Supreme Court lets Trump resume border wall work in Texas's Big Bend
stories.say: The Supreme Court has cleared the way for the Trump administration to restart border wall building in Texas's Big Bend region while a legal challenge goes on.
stories.stand: An unsigned order lifted a lower court's injunction while the case continues; Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson would have refused the government's request.
body: The US Supreme Court has allowed the Trump administration to resume building border wall and related infrastructure in the Big Bend sector of West Texas. The unsigned order on Monday lifted an injunction while the legal challenge continues.
The court said the lower-court order held back the government's interests in border security. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson said she would have denied the request, CBS News reported.

District Judge Kathleen Cardone found last month that the homeland security secretary had exceeded his authority in waiving legal requirements. The challengers, including an environmental group and a river guide, say the project would permanently change a landscape that includes Big Bend National Park.

The Big Bend sector covers more than 500 miles of the southern border. The government says agents caught more than 89,000 people trying to cross there from 2021 to 2025; the plaintiffs say it has the fewest apprehensions of the seven southern sectors.

stories.say: Gadi Eisenkot now has the job of forming Israel's next government, and says he is open to bringing Benjamin Netanyahu into his coalition.
stories.stand: The opposition leader said he was open to Benjamin Netanyahu joining his coalition, after neither bloc won a majority in October's election.
body: Israeli President Isaac Herzog formally tasked opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming the next government on Sunday. Neither bloc won a majority in the 27 October election.
Al Jazeera reported that Eisenkot's four-party alliance won 48 seats and Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc 53. A majority needs 61 seats.

Eisenkot said he was open to Netanyahu, now caretaker prime minister, and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich joining his coalition. He has ruled out governing with Arab-led parties, which won a record 19 seats and endorsed him.
Euronews said a candidate has 28 days to form a government, which the president can extend by up to 14 days. Herzog said Israel needed a stable government.

body: French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has announced that the minimum wage, the SMIC, will rise by 1.6% from 1 December instead of 1 January. Euronews said it will reach about €1,502 a month net, an increase of €24.

Lecornu called it the second largest increase in 20 years but said it was not enough. The CFDT union had sought an extra €100 a month and the CGT about €150.
CGT leader Sophie Binet is calling for another day of strikes and demonstrations on 17 November.

ABC News reported that the S&P 500 rose 2.3% to 7,549 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 2.7% to 25,253. All 11 sectors of the S&P 500 rose, Eurasia Business News said.

stories.head: Boeing to cut 5% of commercial jet workforce as it slows production
stories.stand: Boeing says slower aircraft output has left its commercial airplanes division overstaffed, with layoff notices due to start in December.
stories.say: Boeing is cutting about 5% of staff in its commercial jet business, saying slower production has left it overstaffed, with layoff notices from December.
body: Boeing will cut about 5% of the workforce in its commercial airplanes division, the company told employees on Monday. Layoff notices are expected to start going out in December.

In a memo, division head Stephanie Pope said adjusting production schedules and reducing output had left Boeing overstaffed. The company says factories and suppliers need more time to stabilise before output rises.
AeroTime estimated the cut at roughly 2,500 jobs, based on the division's 50,500 staff at the end of 2025. Some reductions will come through attrition.
Boeing has pushed back its target of building 47 737 jets a month to early 2027. The announcement came about a month after workers approved new contracts that averted a strike, FOX 13 reported.

body: PepsiCo plans to cut about 1,000 jobs in its North American food and beverage business, the Wall Street Journal reported on Monday. The cuts are expected over the following week.
In a letter to staff, PepsiCo North America chief executive Ram Krishnan said the aim was to simplify the company's structure. The company has not confirmed the number of jobs.

stories.say: France's Crédit Agricole has proposed merging its Italian business with Banco BPM to create Italy's third-largest bank, sending Banco BPM shares up about 10%.
body: Crédit Agricole has proposed merging its Italian subsidiary with Banco BPM in what it called a friendly deal. The combined lender would be Italy's third-largest bank.
The French bank already owns 29.6% of Banco BPM and would hold about 45% of the merged group. Banco BPM shareholders would get a 20% valuation premium and a €1bn special dividend.
Crédit Agricole expects about €800m a year in savings. Banco BPM chief executive Giuseppe Castagna would lead the merged bank, and Banco BPM's board will make a first assessment on 12 November.
The deal needs Italy's golden power clearance and other approvals. Crédit Agricole says it could complete in the second half of 2027. Banco BPM shares rose about 10% on Monday.

stories.say: Permanent hiring in the UK fell in October for the first time in four months, recruiters say, as employers held back ahead of the Budget.
body: UK permanent placements fell in October for the first time in four months, according to the KPMG and REC Report on Jobs published on Monday.
The permanent placements index fell to 46.6 from 50.9 in September. Temporary billings also fell, to 48.9. Readings below 50 indicate a decline.
KPMG's Jon Holt said employers pulled back on hiring in the month leading up to the Budget. Starting pay for permanent staff rose more quickly, while candidate availability increased sharply.
London and the north of England saw small rises in permanent placements, while the south of England had the sharpest fall. Demand was strongest for IT and engineering staff.

stories.say: China will keep suspending a 24% extra tariff on American goods for two more months, and has delayed tighter rare-earth export controls until January.
body: China will keep suspending an additional 24% tariff on US imports for two more months, the State Council's Customs Tariff Commission said on Monday. A 10% additional tariff remains in place.
The extension took effect on 10 November. Seoul Economic Daily reported that US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the truce, which had been due to expire on 10 November, now runs to 10 January.

The commission noted US plans to replace tariffs that a court ruled invalid with Section 301 tariffs. China said it would watch US actions and adjust its countermeasures if needed.

stories.say: SpaceX is aiming to launch Starship from Texas on Friday and, for the first time, try to catch both the Super Heavy booster and the upper stage back at the launch tower.
stories.stand: Starship Flight 15 is set to launch from Texas on 13 November, pending FAA approval, with catches of both the booster and the ship planned.
body: SpaceX is targeting Friday 13 November for the 15th flight test of its Starship rocket. It plans to try to catch both stages back at the launch site in South Texas for the first time.
Space.com reported a 75-minute launch window opening at 22:45 GMT. Aviation Week said the date depends on approval from the Federal Aviation Administration.

The Super Heavy booster has been caught on three earlier flights, but the upper stage, called Ship, has never been caught. Space.com said Ship would orbit for more than 22 hours and release 26 Starlink V3 satellites before attempting its catch.
SpaceX says it would call off the catch if anything looked wrong. Flight 14, on 28 September, was Starship's first orbital flight and ended with a splashdown in the northern Pacific.

stories.stand: The DARPA-funded ASTRA robot extended two truss bays and built a third in orbit, which Caltech calls the first autonomous construction in space.
body: A robot built at Caltech has autonomously assembled part of a structure in orbit, the university says. Sergio Pellegrino, who leads the project, called it the first structure autonomously built in space.

The robot, called ASTRA, launched on 30 March on a SpaceX rideshare mission. It extended two pre-assembled bays of a truss and built a third. The full antenna design calls for 11 bays and a reflector about 1.4 metres across.
The team does not expect to finish all 11 bays before the mission ends in December. Caltech says the demonstration still shows the approach is technically feasible.
The work is part of DARPA's NOM4D programme, which explores how to make very large structures in orbit.

stories.stand: The two planets come within a little over one degree of each other in Leo, with closest approach at 02:04 GMT on Monday 16 November.
body: Jupiter and Mars will appear close together in the night sky later this week. Space.com said the closest approach comes at 02:04 GMT on Monday 16 November, citing the In-The-Sky website.

The planets will be a little over one degree apart, roughly the width of a little finger held at arm's length. They sit in the constellation Leo, near the bright star Regulus, with Jupiter the brighter of the two.
Seen from the United States, the pair rises in the east around midnight. A pair of 10x50 binoculars should show both planets in one view.
The planets will then drift apart. Space.com said they will not appear this close again until July 2029.

stories.head: Ancient DNA shows Nazca infant had a rare one-eyed birth condition
stories.say: Researchers say a girl buried about 1,600 years ago in Peru's Nazca region had cyclopia, a rare and fatal condition, caused by an extra copy of chromosome 13.
stories.stand: A 1,600-year-old infant buried in Peru's Palpa Valley had cyclopia linked to trisomy 13, a study in PNAS reports.
body: Researchers say a female infant buried in Peru about 1,600 years ago had cyclopia, a rare and fatal condition that leaves a single central eye socket. The study was published in PNAS on Monday, Live Science reported.
The skeleton came from the Jauranga site in the Palpa Valley, where the Nazca Lines are found. It dates from the Middle Nazca period, A.D. 325 to 440.
DNA analysis found an extra copy of chromosome 13, known as trisomy 13 or Patau syndrome. It is a major known cause of cyclopia, which occurs in about 1 in 100,000 births.

The infant was buried in a ceramic urn with a second girl who had no skeletal abnormalities. Genetic tests showed they had different mothers. Lead author Elsa Tomasto-Cagigao works at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru.

stories.head: Fifth-century warrior graves and buried horses found in Alsace
stories.say: A fifth-century cemetery has been uncovered near Colmar in eastern France, with warriors buried beside decorated weapons and two horses still in their harnesses.
stories.stand: French archaeologists from Inrap uncovered 14 graves and two horse burials near Colmar, including two men buried with richly decorated weapons.
body: Archaeologists in north-eastern France have found a fifth-century cemetery with 14 human graves and two horses buried with their harnesses. The site is at Horbourg-Wihr, near Colmar in Alsace.

The French national archaeology institute, Inrap, excavated the site ahead of a housing project and announced the find on 6 November. The cemetery dates from the second half of the fifth century, on land that held a Roman-era settlement.

Two male graves held swords, shields, javelins and a scramasax short sword, with gold, silver and garnet decoration. Inrap links the weapons to Germanic chiefs or allies of the Roman army, though their identity is unconfirmed. Two female graves held silver bird-shaped brooches and glass bead necklaces.
Some skeletons show blade wounds with no sign of healing, suggesting violent deaths, Live Science and Arkeonews reported. Further study of the injuries is planned.

stories.head: Acorn crops, not deer, best predict Lyme disease ticks, 35-year study finds
stories.say: A thirty-five-year study in New York forests suggests big acorn crops, which feed mice, can signal a rise in Lyme disease ticks about two years later, while deer matter less.
stories.stand: A long-running study in New York forests found heavy acorn years lead to more mice and, about two years on, more ticks that spread Lyme disease.
body: Large acorn crops can forecast a rise in Lyme disease-carrying ticks about two years later, according to a 35-year study published in PNAS. The research was led by Richard Ostfeld at the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in New York.
Heavy acorn years boost white-footed mouse numbers the next year. Years with especially many mice were followed by about 40% more nymphal ticks, the institute said.
Across the full data set, deer numbers showed no statistically significant link to nymph numbers. Newser reported that deer still matter because adult ticks use them to reproduce.

Warmer years were generally followed by fewer nymphs than usual, which the researchers say complicates predictions about climate change. Nearly 500,000 Americans are diagnosed with Lyme disease each year.

stories.head: Peru valley that practised human sacrifice saw little everyday violence
stories.say: Skeletons from Peru's Lambayeque Valley show little everyday violence over about three thousand years, even though its societies practised human sacrifice, a new study finds.
stories.stand: A study of 1,519 skeletons from Peru's Lambayeque Valley found injuries from interpersonal conflict in just 1.6% of people over about 3,000 years.
body: People in Peru's Lambayeque Valley rarely suffered violence from one another over about 3,000 years, despite a history of human sacrifice, a new study suggests. Live Science reported the findings on Monday.

Bioarchaeologists Thomas Snyder of New York University and Haagen Klaus of George Mason University examined the remains of 1,519 people dating from about 1500 B.C. to A.D. 1800. Only 25 people, or 1.6%, had injuries consistent with interpersonal conflict.
Highland societies in Peru showed higher levels of violence. The authors suggest coastal access to seafood and river irrigation may have reduced conflict by securing food supplies.

Klaus suggested ritual violence may have eased everyday conflict, but other researchers noted that sacrifice elsewhere in Peru did not bring the same calm. The study appears in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology.

stories.stand: Laimosemion laranja, an orange-spotted killifish under 3cm long, is known only from pools in Brazil's Amapá state threatened by mining and pollution.
body: Scientists have described a new species of killifish from Brazil's Amazon, named Laimosemion laranja. It is known from only three forest pools in the Rio Cajari drainage in southern Amapá.

Adults are under 3cm long, and males have orange spots and chevrons. The team confirmed the species using body measurements, skeletal features and mitochondrial DNA, according to the publisher Pensoft.
Its total estimated range is 25 square kilometres. One pool lies near water discoloured by mining sediment, and another is in a town and affected by plastic pollution.

The researchers say the fish meets the criteria for Endangered status set by the IUCN. They recommend expanding the Rio Cajari Extractive Reserve to cover its habitat. The study is in Zoosystematics and Evolution.

stories.head: Physicists make an electrically tunable supersolid from light and matter
stories.say: Physicists led by the University of Warsaw have made light and matter behave as a supersolid, both crystal-like and free-flowing, in a device they can tune electrically.
stories.stand: A University of Warsaw-led team observed a supersolid state in exciton polaritons, using a liquid-crystal device that can be tuned electrically.
body: Physicists have observed a supersolid, a state that combines a crystal-like structure with frictionless flow, in a mix of light and matter, the University of Warsaw says. The study is published in Science Advances.

The team used exciton polaritons, hybrid particles of light and matter, inside an optical microcavity containing a liquid crystal and an organic semiconductor. Regularly spaced bright fringes in the emitted light showed a pattern forming on its own.

The fringes shifted from one laser pulse to the next, a sign of spontaneous symmetry breaking. The researchers say their device can be tuned electrically, a first for this kind of supersolid platform.
The work involved the Military University of Technology in Poland, IBM Research Zurich and France's CNRS. Supersolids were first seen in experiments in 2017, using ultracold atoms.

stories.say: Scientists at the European XFEL in Germany have focused ultra-short X-ray pulses into a spot far narrower than a hair, reaching a record intensity for this kind of pulse.
stories.stand: Researchers squeezed hard X-ray pulses of about 300 attoseconds into a spot 180 by 330 nanometres, a record intensity for such pulses.
body: Researchers at the European XFEL facility in Germany say they have produced the most intense hard X-ray attosecond pulses yet. The results are published in the journal Optica.
The pulses lasted an estimated 300 attoseconds. A mirror system focused them onto a spot 180 by 330 nanometres across, about 100,000 times smaller in cross-section than a human hair.

Tests on a thin copper sheet indicated peak intensities above 10^20 watts per square centimetre. Lead author Ichiro Inoue of the University of Tokyo called it a world record in intensity and fluence for such a pulse.
The team aims to study how electrons move in atoms and molecules, and eventually to influence them during chemical reactions. The facility expects its own focusing mirror system in early 2027.

stories.head: Physicists track electrons at a quantum limit on space and time
stories.say: Physicists in Regensburg say an electron's position and timing cannot both be pinned down perfectly, after tracking electrons jumping a tiny gap in attoseconds.
stories.stand: A Regensburg-led team showed an electron's position and timing cannot both be pinned down perfectly, while tracking tunnelling on attosecond scales.
body: Physicists at the University of Regensburg say they have shown a limit on how precisely an electron's position and timing can both be known. The study, with the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg, is in Nature Photonics.
Using laser pulses, the team watched electrons tunnel from a metal tip to a silver surface on attosecond timescales. An attosecond is a billionth of a billionth of a second.
Tighter timing needs more energy, which spreads the electron over a wider region. Simulations showed the electrons lagged the light field by about 500 attoseconds.
The researchers see the work as a step towards electronics far faster than today's chips. That goal has not been demonstrated.

stories.say: Médecins Sans Frontières wants the only Ebola vaccine available at scale used far more widely in Congo, where no vaccine exists for the Bundibugyo strain now spreading.
stories.stand: The medical charity says the vaccine should be freed from research-only limits as Congo's outbreak passes 10,000 confirmed cases.
body: Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) on Monday called for rapid expansion of access to Ervebo, the only Ebola vaccine available at scale, in the Democratic Republic of Congo's Bundibugyo outbreak.

No licensed vaccine exists for the Bundibugyo strain. Ervebo was made for the Zaire strain, but MSF says animal studies suggest it may also protect against Bundibugyo. The charity wants rules tying its use to research protocols lifted.

MSF said Congo and Africa CDC asked in August for 500,000 doses from the global stockpile, but only 70,000 were released. The WHO's vaccine advisers, SAGE, are due to consider a larger release on 17 November.
The WHO reported 10,668 confirmed cases and 5,198 deaths in Congo as of 3 November. Candidate vaccines for Bundibugyo are still being tested, with results months away.

body: Air quality in New Delhi reached severe levels on Monday, a day after Diwali, Al Jazeera reported. The Air Quality Index went above 350 in several parts of the capital.

Residents set off firecrackers through Sunday evening despite restrictions. Last month India's Supreme Court allowed only approved green firecrackers, during three-hour windows on Saturday and Sunday.

body: HIV is spreading beyond high-risk groups into the general population in 27 Russian regions, according to the Central Research Institute of Epidemiology of Rospotrebnadzor, the health watchdog. Euronews reported the findings on Monday.
In these regions HIV is found in more than 1% of pregnant women. Kemerovo, Irkutsk and Sverdlovsk are the worst affected.

Officials also reported a record number of HIV and hepatitis infections in medical facilities in 2025, the highest in 15 years. Euronews said the draft 2027 budget funds medicines for 30,000 new patients.

stories.say: A snapshot count found about 19.5% of patients in UK emergency departments were being treated in corridors or other unsuitable spaces at the start of November.
stories.stand: A snapshot count found about 19.5% of emergency patients in corridors or other unsuitable spaces, the Royal College of Emergency Medicine says.
body: About one in five patients in UK emergency departments were receiving corridor care at the start of November, according to a survey by the Royal College of Emergency Medicine (RCEM). ITV News first reported the results.

Senior A&E staff counted patients at a single moment. About 19.5% were in corridors or other unsuitable spaces, and 88.7% of hospitals had at least one such patient. The share was 27.6% for people in mental health crisis and about 3.5% for children.

RCEM president Dr Ian Higginson called corridor care a stain on the health service. ITV reported that 84% of clinicians surveyed believed patients were coming to harm. ITV also reported that an 81-year-old woman with terminal cancer spent two days in a storeroom at Royal Gwent Hospital in Newport; the health board apologised.

The Department of Health and Social Care told ITV that corridor care has no place in the NHS and that it aims to end it by the end of this Parliament. It is investing £140 million in urgent and emergency care this winter.

Means alleged that former chief of staff Susie Wiles and her deputy, James Blair, pushed health officials to approve fruit-flavoured vapes. He also said officials resisted action on the weedkiller glyphosate, STAT and CBS News reported.

stories.head: About 500 people stuck in South Australian hospitals awaiting aged care beds
stories.say: About 500 people in South Australia are in hospital waiting for an aged care bed, up from 60 four years ago, and the state's health minister wants Canberra to act.
stories.stand: South Australia's health minister wants federal action as the number of hospital patients waiting for aged care places rises from 60 four years ago.
body: About 500 people in South Australia are in hospital waiting for a residential aged care bed, up from 60 four years ago, ABC News reported. The state has the longest residential aged care waits in Australia.

State health minister Blair Boyer said Australia needs at least 10,600 extra federal aged care places a year for the next two decades, but only 800 beds were added last year. He wants the federal government to do more.

A spokesperson for the federal aged care minister called delayed discharge a nationwide challenge. The federal government says it supports about 5,000 new beds a year, including 268 at five Adelaide sites.
The state government hopes a no-interest loan scheme for developers will create 650 beds. It also plans 600 beds at part of the old Women's and Children's Hospital.

body: Nurses and midwives walked off the job at Royal Hobart Hospital and the Repatriation Centre on Saturday, ABC News reported. Hundreds attended a rally over the Tasmanian government's first pay offer.
The offer gives rises of 3%, 2.75% and 2.5% over three years, a total of 8.25%. The current agreement expired in June. Speakers said the offer falls below inflation and would not fix understaffing.

Premier Jeremy Rockliff said the government had worked collaboratively with unions. A government spokesperson said it wanted to resolve the talks quickly.

stories.head: FDA orders vision-loss warning on all GLP-1 diabetes and weight-loss drugs
stories.say: Drugs such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro must now warn of a rare eye condition that can cause sudden and sometimes permanent loss of sight, the FDA said on Monday.
stories.stand: Labels for drugs such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro must warn of NAION, a rare eye condition that can cause permanent sight loss.
body: The US Food and Drug Administration said on Monday that all GLP-1 drugs must carry a warning about a rare eye condition. Non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, can cause sudden and sometimes permanent vision loss.

The drugs, used for type 2 diabetes and obesity, include Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro and Zepbound. The FDA reviewed 126 clinical trials involving more than 134,000 patients, as well as real-world data, Euronews reported.

CBS News reported the FDA found about 6 cases per 100,000 people taking a GLP-1 for at least a year, against under 4 per 100,000 on placebo or other diabetes drugs. The FDA advises anyone with blurred vision or blind spots to seek medical help at once.

Novo Nordisk said the data do not establish cause and effect. Eli Lilly said it was evaluating the update. The European Medicines Agency listed NAION as a very rare side effect of semaglutide last year.

stories.head: Five-year CPR push in North Carolina did not improve cardiac arrest survival
stories.say: Training dispatchers, first responders and more than 200,000 residents across North Carolina did not raise survival after cardiac arrest, a five-year trial found.
stories.stand: Training 911 dispatchers, first responders and 201,586 residents left survival with good brain function at about 9%, the RACE-CARS trial found.
body: A five-year programme to improve the response to cardiac arrest across North Carolina did not increase survival, according to the RACE-CARS trial. Results were presented on Sunday at the American Heart Association meeting in Chicago and published in the New England Journal of Medicine.

The trial covered 60 counties with about 8.5 million people. Intervention counties trained 911 dispatchers and first responders, received 405 defibrillators and ran CPR classes that reached 201,586 people.

Among 22,459 adults who had a cardiac arrest outside hospital, about 9% in intervention counties survived to discharge with good brain function, against 9.4% in control counties. The difference was not significant.

Bystander CPR rates were 44.8% and 42.3%. In the final year, an exploratory analysis found 33% higher odds of bystander CPR in intervention areas. Principal investigator Christopher Granger said sustained outreach may be needed.

stories.head: Novo and Novartis heart drugs fail to cut heart attacks in big trials
stories.say: Novo Nordisk's ziltivekimab and Novartis's pelacarsen both lowered the markers they aimed at, but neither cut heart attacks, strokes or deaths in large trials.
stories.stand: Ziltivekimab lowered inflammation and pelacarsen lowered Lp(a), but neither reduced heart attacks, strokes or deaths, trials at the American Heart Association meeting showed.
body: Two closely watched heart drugs failed to reduce cardiovascular events in large trials presented at the American Heart Association meeting in Chicago and published in the New England Journal of Medicine.

In Novo Nordisk's ZEUS trial, ziltivekimab lowered the inflammatory marker IL-6 but did not cut heart attacks, strokes or cardiovascular deaths. Events occurred in 561 people on the drug and 565 on placebo, News-Medical reported.

Novartis's HORIZON trial found pelacarsen sharply lowered lipoprotein(a), a genetic risk factor carried by about one in five people. But there was no difference in heart attacks, strokes or deaths after almost five years, STAT reported.

ZEUS lead Paul Ridker of Mass General Brigham suggested testing drugs that act earlier in the inflammatory pathway, and in earlier-stage disease. Cardiologists told STAT inflammation remains important.

stories.stand: Long-term follow-up of more than 5,000 patients found death rates of 26% with early procedures and 27% with medicines first.
body: Early stents or bypass surgery do not help people with stable coronary artery disease live longer, according to long-term results of the ISCHEMIA trial. They were presented on Saturday at the American Heart Association meeting and published in JAMA.

The trial enrolled more than 5,000 people at 320 hospitals in 37 countries. Deaths were recorded for up to 13 years. Death rates were 26% in the early-procedure group and 27% in the group given medicines and lifestyle advice first.

Co-lead author Judith Hochman of NYU Langone said early procedures relieve chest pain and improve quality of life but are unlikely to extend life. The team is building tools to tailor decisions to individual patients.

stories.stand: A UK Biobank study of 495,269 adults found coffee drinkers had a 7 to 11% lower risk of the heart rhythm disorder, but it cannot prove cause.
body: People who drank coffee had a 7 to 11% lower risk of atrial fibrillation than non-drinkers, according to a study of 495,269 adults in the UK Biobank. The lowest risk was seen at 2 to 3 cups a day.

The study, by researchers at Zhengzhou University and Peking University, was published in Food & Nutrition Research. Over a median of about 13 years, 37,261 participants developed the heart rhythm disorder.

Drinking 2 to 3 cups of tea a day was linked to about a 5% lower risk. The study is observational and cannot show that coffee or tea prevents atrial fibrillation. Intake was self-reported once, and coffee included decaf.

body: The UN climate summit, COP31, opened in Antalya, Türkiye, on Monday. Negotiators from nearly 200 countries are attending, and the talks run until 20 November.

Türkiye's environment minister, Murat Kurum, took over as COP31 president. PBS NewsHour reported that he said the world will clearly overshoot the 1.5C warming limit, the first COP president to say so. He pledged not to lower ambition and to focus on putting existing commitments into practice.

UN climate chief Simon Stiell told the opening session that progress was too slow and urged countries to speed up solutions. Australia's Chris Bowen is presiding over the negotiations under a shared arrangement with Türkiye. He said the summit's cover decision would hold no surprises.
Climate Home News reported that the agenda was settled after African countries withdrew a request to add items on adaptation finance and trade. Long queues formed at the venue on the first day.

stories.head: 2023 to 2026 set to be the four warmest years on record, WMO says
stories.say: The UN weather agency says 2026 is on track to join the four warmest years ever recorded, with a strengthening El Niño expected to peak in December.
stories.stand: The World Meteorological Organization's update for COP31 also found record sea levels and ocean heat as a strong El Niño builds.
body: The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) published its State of the Climate update on Monday, as COP31 opened. It said 2023 to 2026 are the four warmest years on record.

From January to September 2026, the global average temperature was 1.47C above pre-industrial levels. The record year, 2024, was 1.55C. The WMO expects the full-year figure for 2026 to be higher because of El Niño.

The agency said El Niño has intensified since August and could be the strongest on record by December. Global sea level hit a record high in 2026, and glaciers lost more than 400 gigatons of ice in 2025.

WMO head Celeste Saulo said El Niño does not add new heat to the planet but releases heat stored in the ocean. UN Secretary-General António Guterres said the world had entered a new age of climate extremes.

Spain's weather agency AEMET issued a red warning for heavy rain on Tuesday in the north of Cáceres and the south of Ávila. It warned of extraordinary danger, with a risk of flooding and rising rivers, Infobae reported.
Portugal's IPMA expects gusts of about 100 to 120 km/h on the mainland from Wednesday, with orange warnings. Madeira could see more than 100mm of rain in 12 hours, Euronews reported.
Storm Bruna has already caused flooding in Madeira, leaving ten people homeless, and one person is still missing.

stories.head: Critically endangered frogs rescued after Black Summer fires released
stories.say: Fifty-three southern giant burrowing frogs, raised from tadpoles found after the Black Summer bushfires, have been released into the wild in East Gippsland.
stories.stand: Zoos Victoria bred the species in captivity for the first time after tadpoles were rescued from burnt forest.
body: Fifty-three critically endangered southern giant burrowing frogs have been released into the wild in East Gippsland, Victoria, ABC News reported on Sunday.

The frogs were raised from tadpoles found after the 2019/2020 Black Summer bushfires destroyed their forest habitat. Keepers at Melbourne Zoo and Healesville Sanctuary raised them, and the species bred in captivity for the first time.
Bushfires, drought and the amphibian disease chytridiomycosis have reduced wild numbers. There are fewer than five known breeding sites in Victoria.
Zoos Victoria keeper Meagan Lane said it was the first time the species had been held in any zoo.

stories.head: France blames Iran's Revolutionary Guards for supermarket fridge hacks
stories.say: Jean-Noël Barrot said on Monday that Iran's Revolutionary Guards hacked fridges at about 700 French supermarkets in October. France will seek European sanctions.
stories.stand: France says a Revolutionary Guards cyber unit sabotaged refrigeration at about 700 supermarkets in October, and it will seek European sanctions.
body: France has accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of hacking refrigeration systems in French supermarkets. Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot made the accusation on Monday at G7 talks in Paris.

About 700 of France's 10,000 supermarkets were hit in October, OPB reported. Temperatures reached 50C for about six hours, forcing stores to throw away food. The Record said French authorities counted at least 15 fires.

France's cyber agency, ANSSI, blamed Shahid Kaveh, a cyber unit linked to the Revolutionary Guards. Paris prosecutors have opened a judicial investigation and are seeking international arrest warrants for the unit's leader and two deputies.

France summoned Iran's ambassador and says it will seek European sanctions. Iran had not responded publicly by Monday evening, The Record said. Separate attacks on French blood banks were stopped before any blood was spoiled.

stories.head: Vanderbilt tells campus to shut down devices after cyberattack
stories.say: Vanderbilt University told students and staff on Monday to switch off their devices and leave campus Wi-Fi, as a ransomware group called BYOD claimed to have stolen records.
stories.stand: The Nashville university restricted access to its systems on Monday as a ransomware group called BYOD claimed to have taken student and staff records.
body: Vanderbilt University told students and staff on Monday to shut down university devices and disconnect from campus Wi-Fi after a cyberattack. Its IT team said it was working to contain the incident.

A ransomware group calling itself BYOD claimed responsibility online, The Record and FOX 17 reported. FOX 17 said the group claimed to hold student and employee records, including Social Security numbers. Vanderbilt has not confirmed that any data was taken.

Classes went ahead, FOX 17 said. By Monday evening campus Wi-Fi was back, but most university systems remained restricted. The university said it was working with government agencies and expected normal operations on Tuesday.

Vanderbilt Health, which runs separately, said its IT systems were unaffected so far. BYOD has recently claimed attacks on Michigan State University and the University of New Mexico, The Record reported.

stories.head: Hearing aid firm Amplifon says hackers stole US customers' data
stories.say: Hackers copied names, ID numbers and medical details from hearing care firm Amplifon's US systems early this year. Reports put the number affected at over 1.3 million.
stories.stand: Amplifon's US arm is notifying customers that ID, medical and insurance details were copied in a hack earlier this year.
body: The US arm of Italian hearing care company Amplifon is notifying customers of a data breach. Hackers copied files from its systems between 18 January and 8 February, according to its breach notice.
SecurityWeek and The Record both cite a total of 1,332,826 people affected. Amplifon did not confirm the figure to either outlet.

The stolen data includes names, driver's licence numbers, medical information and health insurance details. Some people's Social Security numbers and financial information were also taken. Amplifon says it is not aware of any fraudulent use of the data.
No hacking group had claimed the attack, The Record said. Amplifon, based in Milan, operates in more than 28 countries.

stories.head: Italy investigates pro-Russian hackers' leak of Tajani's personal data
stories.say: Rome prosecutors are investigating after personal details of Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani were posted on the dark web. A pro-Russian hacker group is blamed.
stories.stand: Rome prosecutors opened a case after details of Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani and other officials were posted on the dark web.
body: Rome prosecutors have opened an investigation into the publication of Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani's personal data on the dark web, ANSA reported on Monday. The probe also covers Ivano Gabrielli, head of Italy's Postal Police.

The leak is attributed to Noname057(16), a pro-Russian hacker group. The Record said the group posted details of 18 European officials and journalists. It offered cryptocurrency for more information about them and their families.

Tajani said the campaign was meant to intimidate him over Italy's support for Ukraine. He later said he was blaming pro-Russian hackers, not the Russian government. The Russian embassy in Italy dismissed the allegations.

A separate probe into leaked data on Rome's chief prosecutor, Francesco Lo Voi, will be handled in Perugia, ANSA said. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed full solidarity with Tajani, Wanted in Rome reported.

stories.head: US adds exploited OpenSSH 'SSHole' flaw to urgent patch list
stories.say: America's cyber defence agency added the OpenSSH bug on Monday to its list of flaws under attack. Very long passwords can unlock accounts on Alpine Linux and similar systems.
stories.stand: CISA listed the login-bypass bug as actively exploited on Monday, as attacks on Alpine Linux and other musl-based systems grow.
body: The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added an OpenSSH flaw known as SSHole to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on Monday. Federal agencies were given until 12 November to patch, SecurityOnline reported.

The bug, CVE-2026-123158, lets an attacker log in to accounts that should have no password by sending a very long password. It affects OpenSSH before version 10.6p2 on Linux systems built with the musl C library and without PAM, such as Alpine Linux.

Security firms say exploitation is growing. Previdian confirmed root access on an Alpine Linux honeypot, Help Net Security reported. Cyber Daily said GreyNoise saw its first successful exploitation on 7 November, from a Chinese IP address.
A fix was released on 5 November. Systems using the glibc library, such as Debian and Ubuntu, are not affected. Administrators must restart the SSH service after updating.

stories.say: Anthropic released two new Claude models on Monday, saying they respond up to 30% faster. Fable 5.2's input price drops from 10 dollars to 8 per million tokens.
stories.stand: The AI company says its new models are up to 30% faster, and it cut Fable 5.2's input price as it prepares to go public.
body: Anthropic released two new AI models, Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, on Monday. The company says they improve on coding, reasoning and vision and respond up to 30% faster.
Fable 5.2's input price falls from $10 to $8 per million tokens, TechCrunch reported. Gulf News said output costs $40 per million tokens. Both models are built on the same underlying system.

Fable 5.2 is widely available but has safeguards that block most cybersecurity and biology tasks, Malay Mail reported, citing AFP. Mythos 5.2 has fewer limits and is offered only to vetted cybersecurity and life-sciences organisations.

Anthropic said both models voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than recent models. It warned this could make real-world behaviour harder to predict. Its system card says Mythos 5.2 shows stronger covert capabilities than earlier Claude models on several tests.

stories.head: Norway pauses new grid bookings for data centres amid AI boom
stories.say: Norway's grid operator Statnett stopped taking new power reservations for data centres on Monday, and the government says it will bring in licences for them.
stories.stand: Grid operator Statnett halted new connection reservations for data centres until as late as August 2027, as the government plans licences.
body: Norway's grid operator, Statnett, has temporarily stopped taking new grid capacity reservations for data centres. It announced the pause on Monday and expects to lift it by 1 August 2027 at the latest.

Statnett said 800 MW of data centres are connected, 4,200 MW are reserved and 9,100 MW are in the queue. Requests for a further 18,000 MW have been made. Norway's peak power use is just over 25,000 MW.
Statnett says it needs time to set technical rules, citing data centres' large and rapid swings in power use. Existing connections are not affected.

The government said it plans a licensing scheme for data centres, giving priority to defence, police, health and critical infrastructure. Energy Minister Terje Aasland said data centres made up 75% of the 26,000 MW of new connection requests this year.

body: Disney and Adobe announced a multi-year AI alliance on Monday, making Adobe Disney's official AI innovation partner. Disney gets early access to new Adobe AI and creative tools.

Adobe will use its Firefly Foundry service to build custom generative models trained on Disney's characters, environments and visual styles. The companies say the aim is commercially safe, production-ready output.

Mediaweek said Disney invested $1bn in OpenAI in December 2025 and licensed characters for its Sora video app. The Decoder reported that Disney later withdrew from that deal.
